entries.title: Bulls' offense won't change without Caleb Wilson
entries.summary: <p>With one win in the Bulls’ first 10 games, fans were coming to grips with the idea that this season would be about Caleb Wilson’s development and his pursuit of the NBA Rookie of the Year award.</p><p>Both are on hold after Wilson, the fourth overall pick in the draft, had surgery Thursday for a broken right hand he suffered Wednesday against the Spurs. For at least a month, fans will have to put their focus on something else — and that won’t be easy on this team.</p><p>Wilson entered the game Friday against the Hawks as the Bulls’ second-leading scorer, averaging 18.9 points, just behind team leader Norman Powell (19.3). Among rookies, Wilson was third in scoring, first in steals per game (1.8) and second in blocked shots (0.9). He was among the early leaders for the top rookie honor.</p><p>“To see a guy that’s just come in, he’s played 10 games in the NBA, he’s playing really well and then to get injured like that, it sucks,” Josh Giddey said.</p><p>“He’s frustrated, just like all of us,” coach Tiago Splitter said.</p><p>Wilson has been unlucky with his hand health. At North Carolina, he broke his left hand in February, and after being cleared to work out, he broke his right thumb on a dunk in March. It’s widely believed that had Wilson not gotten hurt, he wouldn’t have fallen to the Bulls.</p><p>That’s one break that went the Bulls’ way. Splitter said he asked Wilson about his rash of hand injuries.</p><p>“It’s just bad luck, a freak injury,” Splitter said. “Just have to be patient.”</p><p>The Bulls hadn’t been so patient on the court with Wilson. They had been throwing a lot at him, and he had been responding with not just numbers but development. He also had been jelling with his teammates in Splitter’s uptempo offense.</p><p>Now that offense, which finally has been working as it's supposed to — better shooting certainly has helped — is without a key cog. But Splitter said he won’t change the offense, though others will have to make up for the team-high 16 shots Wilson took per game.</p><p>“Of course, we’re going to miss him, but it doesn’t change what we want to do,” Splitter said. “Everybody else is going to have more shots. I don’t expect just one guy to be more aggressive. Naturally, the game’s going to find the shots, and the players are going to take those shots. I’m not worried about that.”</p><p>“It’s a big hole to fill,” Giddey said. “He was very productive for us on both sides of the ball. I don’t think it’s as simple as just putting someone in to replace Caleb. It’s going to have to be by committee. It allows opportunities for other guys to come in and play a bigger role.”</p><p>Two of those players will be big men Nic Claxton and Jalen Smith, who Splitter said will see more time together now that Claxton is closer to playing normal minutes. He was restricted to about 16-20 minutes in his first two games back from a hamstring injury that cost him a month. Splitter said the team wants him to play about 20-24 minutes.</p><p>Fortunately for the Bulls, Powell returned from back spasms that kept him out of two games. The veteran guard entered the game averaging the second-most shots on the team with 13, though he had made only 40% of them, 70 points below his career average.</p><p>As for Wilson, Splitter said he’ll stay involved with the team, being at practice and watching video. Splitter said that was important for Wilson, as well as seeing the game from a different perspective. With a hand injury, he’ll be able to stay in shape, though not exactly game shape. Splitter had an idea interesting idea for Wilson.</p><p>“Maybe work on the left hook or something like that,” he said.</p>

entries.title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop. O'Hare, Midway flights can resume after hours of delays, cancellations
entries.summary: <p>Hours after the Federal Aviation Administration halted flights across the country Friday, including at Midway and O'Hare airports, the agency said departures can resume.</p><p>Officials blamed “an incredibly old air traffic control system" for instability in air traffic control communications during a White House briefing Friday evening.</p><p>Inside O’Hare International Airport — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/01/20/ohare-reclaims-top-spot-named-nations-busiest-airport-in-2025" target="_blank" >the busiest airport in the U.S.</a> — confused passengers wandered around as luggage piled up on baggage carousels. Long lines of travelers rummaged through hundreds of bags from flights that never took off because of the delay.</p><p>The FAA grounded all flights nationwide at around 2:36 p.m., and an FAA alert said the stoppage was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." They said they lifted the ground stop at 7:15 p.m., though it was unclear when flights actually would resume.</p><p>A sudden silence fell over O'Hare as travelers were notified that the ground stop had been lifted. But a video board displaying flight information still showed delays or cancellations even though many passengers attempted to buy tickets at nearby airline kiosks. </p><p>"For an 18-hour trip back and forth, it doesn't make sense for us and try to go," said Angelica Colmenares, who was en route to Paris for a 48-hour trip with a friend. Luckily, we were flying standby so we didn't fly, but now we're going to have our own party in Chicago."</p><p>Some airlines, including JetBlue and Air Canada, had already said they were canceling the rest of their Friday night flights.</p><p>U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the public was "never in danger" and the flights were grounded due to an "abundance of caution."</p><p>By 5:30 p.m., O'Hare had reported 328 flight cancellations and 847 delays. Midway saw 30 canceled flights and 186 delays, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.flychicago.com/business/media/delays/pages/default.aspx" target="_blank" >Chicago Department of Aviation</a>. </p><p>As of 6:15 p.m. on Friday, 30 flights scheduled to arrive at O'Hare since 2:55 p.m. had been diverted. Ten arrivals scheduled at Midway were also diverted. </p><p>U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communication issue affected all of the nation's 22 air traffic control centers that route planes between airports.</p><p>During the evening briefing, Duffy shifted focus to a political fight, saying the Trump administration had been “asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system.”</p><p>Mullin said there was no sign yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."</p><p>“Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying,” he said.</p><p>Although the order was lifted, Duffy said he expected it to take a bit to catch up on flight schedules. “Hopefully tomorrow, we are going to start to see far better movement,” he said.</p><p>Earlier at O'Hare, video boards displaying flight information were checkered with red and yellow, signifying the delays and cancellations that forced many travelers to book hotel rooms for the night or rent a car to arrive at their destinations.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: CPS faces possible midyear budget cuts as unexpected funding costs mount
entries.summary: <p>Just a few months into the school year, Chicago Public Schools has overspent its budget and its emergency contingency budget for special education by $27 million — one of several “compounding financial pressures” that could mean midyear cuts if the school district doesn’t get more from the state in the state Legislative veto session that starts Tuesday.</p><p>Besides ballooning special education costs, CPS officials say they had to pay more than expected in interest on short-term loans to make payroll and received $19 million less in state funding than expected.</p><p>And these unexpected costs don’t even include the staff that CPS rehired this fall at the direction of school board members aligned with the Chicago Teachers Union. In a controversial move, these members approved a last-minute budget amendment counting on $150 million more from the state, even though it had yet to be committed.</p><p>The district only wound up re-hiring some of the staff laid off — 128 teachers and 153 support staff at a cost of $29 million. District officials are already planning to re-lay off those staff members as early as Dec. 1 if no additional money comes through, according to a memo obtained by the Chicago Tribune.</p><p>But district officials have yet to say how they plan to handle the other costs that are creating a hole in the district’s budget.</p><p>“The CPS Finance team is closely monitoring our budget, assessing implications of rising costs and a shortfall if no additional state revenue is received, and identifying potential solutions,” CPS officials said in a statement. “CPS will continue to keep our Board and community apprised of any additional financial savings that will need to be enacted this school year.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Bulls get long-awaited second victory in first game without Caleb Wilson
entries.summary: <p>It looked as though the Bulls were going to let another big lead get away when their 18-point edge over the Hawks disappeared. But they kept it together, and <b>Norman Powell</b> took over by scoring nine of his 33 points in overtime to lead them to a 125-117 victory for their long-awaited second triumph of the season.</p><p>For a team that entered the day on an eight-game skid, the Bulls (2-9) showed a lot of fight during the game and a lot of emotion as it ended.</p><p>‘‘It’s not easy to lose a lot of games,’’ coach <b>Tiago Splitter</b> said. ‘‘You’ve got to stay composed; you’ve got to stay locked in. But that frustration’s still there. And when you win a game, sometimes that stuff comes out.’’</p><p><b>Josh Giddey</b> had his first triple-double of the season with 15 points, 10 rebounds and 14 assists. The Bulls had 34 assists for the game — evidence of the way Splitter wants to play, with or without rookie <b>Caleb Wilson</b>, who missed his first of many games with a broken right hand.</p><p>The Bulls got plenty of contributions, with seven players scoring in double figures. <b>Isaac Okoro</b> and <b>Jalen Smith</b> also scored 15 points, <b>Patrick Williams</b> had 13, <b>Buddy Hield</b> 12 and <b>Matas Buzelis</b> 11, including a big three-pointer with 23.5 seconds left in overtime that gave the Bulls a six-point lead.</p><p>And for those interested, the Bulls put themselves in the running for at least a wild-card spot in the NBA Cup. The victory put them in a three-way tie for second with the Wizards and Hawks in East Group C at 1-1. With winnable remaining games against the Wizards and Hornets, a 3-1 record is possible.</p><h3>Robinson fills out roster</h3><p>The Bulls signed center <b>Orlando Robinson</b> from their G League affiliate, Windy City, to fill their 15th and final standard-contract roster spot. With a full roster, the Bulls’ two-way players — <b>Tobe Awaka</b>, <b>Jordan Hawkins</b> and <b>Jaylin Sellers</b>, who split time with Windy City — are eligible to play in 50 games each, rather than 90 combined.</p><p>Splitter said Robinson earned the spot. He averaged 13.7 points and eight rebounds in three games for Windy City. He also played in three preseason games for the Bulls, averaging 6.3 points and 4.3 rebounds. The 26-year-old has appeared in 115 NBA games in four seasons, playing for the Heat, Kings, Raptors and Magic.</p><p>‘‘Orlando was great for us in camp,’’ Splitter said. ‘‘He’s a great spirit on the bench, always good vibes. Our guys love him. It’s a reward from the camp that he had for us.’’</p><h3>Still a happy place</h3><p>Despite all the Bulls’ losing, Giddey said he and his teammates still enjoy coming to work and are putting in the effort to improve.</p><p>‘‘Clearly, we’re not up to where we should be,’’ he said. ‘‘Teams are showing us that, and we’ve got to be able to put 48 minutes together. But the group’s positive, the building’s positive. It’s a place I love to come in every day and see everybody and work. We all have the same goal of getting back to winning games.’’</p><p>If they don’t, the season might be historically bad. The Bulls are on pace to win 15 games, which would equal the franchise low for a full season, set in 2000-01. The Bulls won 13 games in the lockout-shortened 1988-89 season.</p><h3>Historic achievement</h3><p>Big men <b>Nic Claxton</b> and <b>Jalen Smith</b> each had at least 17 points and an 83.3 field-goal percentage Wednesday against the Spurs. It was the first time in team history two centers put up those numbers in the same game. Smith had 23 points and shot 88.9%.</p>

entries.title: New Trier's Throy Nightingale runs for 5 TDs, 309 yards in emotional state quarterfinal win against Huntley
entries.summary: <p>New Trier’s football team learned that classmate Brock Beeler had died as they took the field to practice on Wednesday.</p><p>“It is hard watching 17- and 18-year-olds find that news out,” Trevians coach Brian Doll said. “We just needed to be there for them. Football is football, but life is life. We needed to do something for our kids that day and support them. I canceled practice right when I found out. It was a tough decision but the right decision.”</p><p>“It was the right move,” New Trier senior Harry Resis said. “A lot of our captains were really close with Brock, and we needed some time to reset and think about what happened. And just grieve together.”</p><p>Beeler played football his sophomore year, and his jersey hung on the sideline on Friday night in Huntley as the Trevians beat the Red Raiders 42-28 in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/10/17/ihsa-state-football-playoff-pairings-class8a-illinois-2026" >Class 8A</a> quarterfinal.</p><p>“It just means a lot that we can get a win in his honor and bring everyone together and make the community feel a little better in a time of sadness and loss,” Resis said.</p><p>Resis, a tight end, and linemen Nicholas Danielsen and Sean Feeney were part of a New Trier rushing attack that overwhelmed undefeated Huntley (11-1).</p><p>Senior running back Throy Nightingale Jr. carried the load, rushing 39 times. He finished with a career-high 309 yards and scored five touchdowns.</p><p>“It’s a great feeling getting support [from the line],” Nightingale said. “It was amazing getting support from them. They said to keep going, and I kept going.”</p><p>Nightingale transferred to New Trier from Notre Dame this year, but still knew Beeler.</p><p>“It was definitely tough,” Nightingale said. “[Beeler] would be here right now, and I know he would want us to keep going and to keep pushing. So we did that for him tonight.”</p><p>The Trevians (11-1) led 21-0 in the second quarter after Nightingale’s second TD run.</p><p>Huntley pulled within 21-14 early in the second half on a 10-yard touchdown pass from Malik Carter to Matthew Schroeder. But that was as close as it would get.</p><p>“[New Trier] took it to us today in all three phases, really,” Red Raiders coach Mike Naymola said. “They were a lot more physical than us. I was proud of what these guys were able to do. We were resilient and fought back, and right when we got ourselves back in the game they made another play.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: No. 3 Illini get back to winning ways vs. Sam Houston
entries.summary: <p>Tomislav Ivisic had a career-high 28 points, Andrej Stojakovic added 26 and No. 3 Illinois bounced back from its first loss this season with a 108-86 victory over Sam Houston on Friday night in Champaign.</p><p>Coming off an 84-78 defeat Tuesday night at No. 16 Texas Tech, the Fighting Illini (3-1) pulled away from the Bearkats by scoring 63 points in the second half to set up a high-profile showdown with No. 2 Duke next week.</p><p>After trailing 45-40 at halftime, Sam Houston (2-2) went in front 57-56 with 15:58 left on a fast-break dunk by Enel St. Bernard. Ivisic answered 14 seconds later with a 3-pointer that launched an 11-0 run for the Illini, who never trailed again.</p><p>Ivisic scored 10 of the first 14 points for Illinois in the second half. He briefly left the court midway through the period after being elbowed in the mouth, but returned and finished the game.</p><p>Stefan Vaaks scored 14 points off the bench, and Quentin Coleman had 11 points, eight rebounds and six assists for Illinois. Ethan Brown also scored 11.</p><p>Justin Begg had 19 points and 10 assists for the Bearkats. Aidan McDowell also scored 19 points, Yoda Oke added 14 off the bench and Jacobe Coleman finished with 11.</p><p>The Illini forced 14 turnovers, converting them into 19 points, and had nine steals and six blocks.</p><p>Illinois is 3-0 at home and has scored at least 108 points in all three blowouts.</p><p>It was the first game between Illinois and Sam Houston, but Illini coach Brad Underwood improved to 9-0 against the Bearkats. The first eight wins came in the Southland Conference from 2013-16 when Underwood was the coach at Stephen F. Austin.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Sam Houston visits Wyoming on Tuesday.</p><p>Illinois plays at No. 2 Duke on Tuesday.</p><p></p><p><b>DePAUL 67, NORTHWESTERN 47</b></p><p>Kruz McClure scored 18 points and Koree Cotton added 15 as DePaul defeated crosstown foe Northwestern 67-47 on Friday night.</p><p>The Blue Demons (4-0) took down the Wildcats (3-1) for the first time since Dec. 21, 2019, and the first time in Evanston since Dec. 27, 2013. Northwestern had not trailed at any point in three previous games.</p><p>DePaul shot just 36% as a team and 31% from deep, but held Northwestern to 31% and 25% marks. The Blue Demons hit 11 3-pointers, their third straight game in double-figures.</p><p>Fabian Flores grabbed eight rebounds, and Cotton and Magoon Gwath each had six. Layden Blocker had two blocks and two steals.</p><p>The two teams traded the lead back-and-forth in a low-scoring first half, and DePaul led 27-23 at the break. entries.title: Illini come up short against No. 4 UCLA
entries.summary: <p>PASADENA, Calif. — Ty Dieffenbach threw for 232 yards and two touchdowns and overcame a left shoulder injury that sidelined him, and No. 4 UCLA remained unbeaten with a rain-soaked, 22-14 victory over Illinois on Friday night.</p><p>Aiden Mizell had six catches for 176 yards and a touchdown, and Semaje Morgan added 56 yards receiving and a score for the Bruins (10-0, 7-0 Big Ten, No. 4 CFP). Scooter Jackson had two interceptions, the last with 2:50 left to stymie the Illini (6-4, 4-3).</p><p>UCLA started a season 10-0 for the third time in program history.</p><p>Dieffenbach left with 35 seconds to go in the first half after he fell hard on his shoulder following a hit by defensive lineman Carter Janki. Third-stringer Madden Iamaleava played the next three series for the Bruins as Dieffenbach remained in the locker room.</p><p>Dieffenbach returned with 55 seconds left in the third quarter. He led UCLA on a seven-play, 75-yard scoring drive on his first drive back, capped by a 26-yard touchdown pass to Morgan.</p><p>Dieffenbach, a senior transfer from Cal Poly, completed 13 of 20 passes and improved to 5-0 as the Bruins' starting quarterback. He became the starter after Nico Iamaleava, the older brother of Madden Iamaleava, sustained a season-ending knee injury against Oregon on Oct. 10.</p><p>The Bruins had three interceptions, a fumble recovery and a safety while limited Illinois to 240 yards. UCLA has held seven straight opponents to 20 points or less and upped its season total to 31 takeaways, most in the nation.</p><p>Katin Houser went 16 of 34 for 176 yards with two touchdowns and three interceptions for the Illini, who saw their four-game winning streak snapped. Kaden Feagin caught an 18-yard touchdown pass and Collin Dixon hauled in a 7-yard touchdown pass.</p><p>The Bruins jumped out to a 10-0 halftime lead. On just the fifth play of the game, Dieffenbach hit Mizell on a 54-yard touchdown strike down the sideline. It was Mizell’s third straight reception that resulted in a touchdown after he had two 75-yard scores against Maryland last week.</p><p>Mateen Bhaghani added a 20-yard field goal with 1:26 remaining before halftime. UCLA got the ball back for one more possession, but Dieffenbach went down and left the game with a trainer to end any hopes of another score before the break.</p><p>Aiden Gobaira sacked Houser in the end zone for a safety to extend the Bruins’ lead in the third quarter. After Illinois scored its first with a touchdown to cut it to 12-7, Dieffenbach returned and found Morgan early in the fourth quarter to re-extend the lead.</p><p>Houser connected with Dixon with 7:14 remaining to bring Illinois within a touchdown at 19-14. The Illini forced a three-and-out to get the ball back and had a chance to take the lead, but Jackson intercepted Houser's pass with 2:50 remaining.</p><p>Bhagnani kicked 37-yard field goal and Illinois’ last-gasp attempt ended with a turnover on downs at its own 33.</p><p>Houser was injured on the Illini’s final drive and replaced by backup Carson Boyd.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Illinois: The Illini have attained bowl eligibility and will try to bounce back against Iowa next Saturday.</p><p>UCLA: The Bruins remain in the driver’s seat for a top College Football playoff berth. Their 10-game winning streak tied a school record.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Illinois: Hosts Iowa on next Saturday.</p><p>UCLA: At Michigan next Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Why Chicago dog owners should register their canines and how to do it
entries.summary: <p>Only a tiny fraction of Chicago’s dogs have city licenses, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/06/chicago-dog-licenses-all-time-low-city-clerk-anna-valencia" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times</u></a> article last week. So why should owners license their dogs?</p><p>Chicago actually requires all dogs four months or older to be registered with the city. However, this is not well-enforced, said Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd).</p><p>The city clerk’s office has issued only 4,100 dog licenses this year in Chicago, which has an estimated dog population of more than 650,000. That’s down from 8,000 dog licenses last year, 18,000 in 2017 and 40,896 in 2013.</p><p>And for canines that use off-leash “dog-friendly areas,” Chicago Park District also requires a separate $10 permit per dog (see below).</p><p><b>What’s the benefit of licensing dogs?</b></p><p>Registering a dog helps the city locate its owner if a pet gets lost. “If your pet escapes and has a valid city license tag on it, the city will take the dog home for free,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/06/chicago-dog-licenses-all-time-low-city-clerk-anna-valencia" target="_blank" ><u>Ald. Ray Lopez</u></a> (15th) told the Sun-Times. It won’t go to Animal Care and Control.</p><p>The person who finds the dog calls the city clerk’s office at 312-744-DOGS with the canine’s registration number on its ‘emblem’ – a sticker that goes on a dog tag.</p><p>In addition, registration is required to stay at many dog boarding and daycare service facilities and for entering the Chicago Park District's dog-friendly areas.</p><p><b>How much does registration cost?</b></p><p>For decades, the license fee has been $5 a year for spayed and neutered dogs, $50 for those that are not and $2.50 for dog owners who are senior citizens.</p><p><b>What do you need to register a dog? How do I get a license?</b></p><p>Dogs must have a current rabies vaccination for a license.</p><p>Owners can register <a class="Link" href="https://ezbuy.chicityclerk.com/" target="_blank" >online</a> through the city clerk’s website by uploading a dog’s vaccination document and paying by credit card. It takes up to 12 business days to receive a dog license emblem via U.S. mail. If an owner needs the tag immediately, they can go to an <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicityclerk.com/contact-us" target="_blank" >in-person sales location.</a></p><p><b>How long do dog licenses last?</b></p><p>The city offers 1-year and 3-year emblems since rabies vaccinations typically last either one or three years.</p><p><b>What’s the penalty if a dog doesn’t have a license or permit?</b></p><p>There is a $500 fine for using a dog-friendly area without a permit.</p><p>The city clerk’s website doesn’t list penalties for unregistered dogs and a spokesperson said Animal Care and Control handles enforcement. But <a class="Link" href="https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/chicago/latest/chicago_il/0-0-0-2640432" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago code</u></a> states that fines for unregistered dogs can range from $30 to $200 for each day of violation. However, fines don’t seem well-enforced given the number of unregistered dogs in Chicago.</p><p><b>How do I get a Chicago Parks District permit for off-leash areas? </b></p><p>For a <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/facilities/dog-friendly-areas#2272436614-2789263867-1" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Park District</u></a> permit for dog-friendly areas in parks and beaches, the owner must have a city dog license or proof of current rabies vaccination. The owner must also have veterinary documents showing tests for parasites and vaccination for six diseases, including distemper. Permits cost $10 per dog.</p><p>Applications are available at about 50 participating veterinarian offices <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/facilities/dog-friendly-areas#2272436614-2789263867-1" target="_blank" ><u>listed here</u></a>.</p><p><b>Why don’t Chicago pet owners register their dogs?</b></p><p>City Clerk Anna Valencia said most Chicago dog owners don’t know that they’re required to buy city licenses. The city doesn’t have a marketing budget to raise awareness about the issue, she said.</p>

entries.summary: <p>Nothing puts me in the mood to bike like the fall. Colder weather makes me think of the coming winter. I get FOMO and take out the bike.</p><p>But where to go? The hill there has one of the best views of the skyline. A former quarry and then a trash mound, the city turned it into a park in 2009.</p><p>This park, with its prairie grass and a fish-stocked pond, is a great entry point for Bridgeport, one of the city's oldest neighborhoods. Bridgeport is home to immigrants, artists and some of the most old-school Chicagoans you’ll ever meet. Its name comes from river barge captains forced to unload their cargo at the Ashland Avenue bridge because it was too low to the river.</p><p>I lived a block west of Palmisano Park when I moved to Chicago 12 years ago. Back then, Palmisano was my go-to spot — for a picnic, and for the Fourth of July, when crowds would gather to catch 360-degree views of fireworks across the city. It was also my scenic cut-through to the Orange Line’s Halsted station.</p><p>That station is a great way to get to the neighborhood, if you’re coming from far away. You could also bike Halsted Street itself. The street recently got decent bike lanes, stretching up to Greek Town and down to 59th Street.</p><p>Next, let's head east on 29th Street.</p><h4><b>Impallaria Bakery and Deli, 2952 S. The eclairs are my mom's favorite.</p><p>As you continue south, notice how some homes appear sunken below street level. They were built before the city raised its streets and downtown in the mid-1800s to allow for sewers. entries.title: How we photographed a Chicago truck driver's pro sumo wrestling debut
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from photojournalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tyler-pasciak-lariviere" target="_blank" >Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere</a>. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/TylerLaRiviere" target="_blank" >X</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://bsky.app/profile/tylerplariviere.bsky.social" target="_blank" >Blue Sky</a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/tylerpasciaklariviere/" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>This image showcases a sumo wrestler from the Chicago area clashing with a fellow wrestler in a new professional U.S.-based sumo wrestling league. This event was the league’s second ever event since its inception. So being on the ground level and witnessing the spectacle and ritual of sumo wrestling — and the scrappiness of this league and its potential — was exciting.</p><h3>How I got this photo:</h3><p>One of the biggest surprises when covering sumo wrestling for the first time was just how fast this combat sport is. Most bouts only last mere seconds as wrestlers using their own techniques do their best to push their opponents out of the dohyō, or ring, or send them to the floor. A production photographer who photographed practice rounds earlier in the day gave me the rundown: telling me about the different rituals that go into a fight and explaining where to be so I wouldn't be in the way of the production team or fighters. He told me to constantly watch the fights and warned that I should be ready to flee if a fighter comes tumbling toward you. I took off my boots and took my position on the boundary mat as close to the center of the ring as possible.</p><p>Sumo has a lot of rituals that helped me as a photographer get ready for the action. Fights don’t start until both fighters come into the ring, show respect with a bow, give some form of a respectful taunt to one another (each unique to the fighter), and put both fists onto the mat. The gyōji, or ref, then gives a yell to signal the fight to begin. Fortunately, the fighter featured in the photo above was later on during the event, so I had time to dial in my shooting settings and get a sense of what was to come. But sumo is full of surprises. It's the only combat sports without weight classes and some of the wrestlers, who could be around 400 pounds up, can still lose bouts against fighters half their weight.</p><p>The fight represented in the photos was Elgin fighter Ruperto Cintron's third and final fight of the night. He lost his other two matches, and his opponent Jabari Webb was on the attack immediately after the fight commenced, pushing Cintron towards the left edge of the ring. Cintron did what he could, which was attempt to throw Webb out of the ring using Webb’s momentum against him. However, despite Webb being thrown out of the ring, Cintron touched the mat outside the ring first and lost his third bout for the night eliminating him from that event's tournament. entries.title: Send Jeffries, Schumer packing and vote in leaders who will deliver
entries.summary: <p>It’s not surprising that the political wrestling has begun in the U.S. House and Senate as to who the new leadership should be. The newly elected Democrat representatives won on progressive promises they put themselves on the line for and they cannot and will not compromise their values. In my opinion, Hakeem Jeffries disqualified himself when he said that he would <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/meet-the-press/video/hakeem-jeffries-says-medicare-for-all-is-not-legislation-he-currently-supports-268371525570" target="_blank" >not support</a> Medicare for All. And Mr. <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/6210724-ocasio-cortez-declines-schumer-support/" target="_blank" >Chuck Schumer </a>would have to do a real turnaround to be considered for leadership, which would demand fighting for policies he has not been strong for thus far.</p><p>The names of who will lead the House and Senate aren't as important as the policies they must commit to. Any leadership to be considered must be totally committed to these things for starters:<br></p><ol class="rte2-style-ol" id="rte-0051e7a1-dd3c-11f1-81ad-3d7a87bf6d28" start="1"><li>Ending the war with Iran</li><li>Stop funding the genocide in Gaza</li><li>Restoring the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program</li><li>Funding healthcare</li><li>Medicare for All</li><li>Raising the minimum wage</li></ol><p>In my opinion, no one who seeks leadership should be considered without committing to these mandates. The days for personal power and position must end. The people have spoken, and now the elected officials must put the people first.</p><p><i>The Rev. Michael L. Pfleger, senior pastor, Faith Community of St. Sabina Church</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-0f0000" name="module-0f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>New lawmakers must press Jeffries </h3><p>Later this week, U.S. House Democrats will choose their leadership, and Hakeem Jeffries is running for speaker unopposed. Chicago’s incoming U.S. representatives, including <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-house-illinois-midterm-results" >Patty Garcia</a>, shouldn't treat that vote as a formality.</p><p>Jeffries’ instinct again and again has been to protect the leadership structure first and fight second. In March 2025, after Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer handed Republicans the <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/senate/5194440-schumer-liberals-gop-government-funding-bill/" target="_blank" >votes</a> for a six-month blank check, Jeffries refused to say whether Schumer should stay. But after the shutdown collapsed that November, he broke his silence and expressed support for Schumer. Jeffries waited months after the New York City mayoral primary to endorse Zohran Mamdani — then the Democratic nominee<b> —</b> finally doing so the <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/24/after-a-lengthy-wait-jeffries-to-endorse-mamdani-00621799" target="_blank" >day before early voting</a>.</p><p>Yes, Democrats just won the House. But winning an election against Donald Trump is not the same as governing against him, and the record shows how Jeffries folds under pressure.</p><p>The leadership ballot is secret, but nothing stops a new member from saying what he or she expects of a speaker before casting a vote. Our incoming representatives should ask Jeffries for specific commitments on how he’ll use this majority, and say publicly what they heard.</p><p>Chicago sent fighters to Washington, D.C. Their first vote should prove it.</p><p><i>Troy Gould, Heart of Chicago</i></p><h3>No action Jackson </h3><p>I wonder what U.S. Rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., had to do on Tuesday that was so important that he missed the impeachment vote on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The measure failed by seven votes. Eleven Democrats were absent. No wonder people are angry with the Democratic Party.</p><p><i>Tom Kosinski, Ravenswood Gardens</i></p><h3>Living up to Lincoln</h3><p>If President Abraham Lincoln is looking down on us right now, he must be pleased.</p><p>In our midterm elections, this nation gave birth to new freedom. A "government of the people, by the people, for the people" didn't perish from the Earth. Competent candidates defeated special interests. Black, Native American and Latina candidates made history. Abdul El-Sayed and Chris Pappas won Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire, respectfully.</p><p>America is a work in progress. We still have much to do to make this a country that truly exercises “with liberty and justice for all.”</p><p>At Gettysburg, Lincoln expressed a belief in our country’s future. In this election cycle, we have kept the faith.</p><p><i>William Dodd Brown, Lincoln Square</i></p><h3>Stay patient </h3><p>I applaud reader Eli Washington for his<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/11/11/veterans-educational-opportunities-trump-midterms-measles-sexual-assault-house-speaker-blackhawks" > letter</a> in Wednesday's Sun-Times. I too want to remind everyone change will not happen overnight. We need to remain calm. Donald Trump is still president and says he will work with Democrats, but I think that is doubtful.</p><p><i>Virginia Dare McGraw, Naperville</i></p><h3>Welcome back, America</h3><p>The blue tidal wave established that no matter what party, what religion, what social persuasion, united we stand. Black people, Asians, Native Americans, women, youth, Latinos, whites, "Dreamers," seniors ALL count. With the exception of Native Americans, we all are descendants of immigrants. Yet together we ARE the blue tidal wave and we matter. Congratulations, my fellow Americans. Well done.</p><p><i>Jude Smallwood, Royal Palm Beach, Florida</i></p><h3>Not sitting pretty after blocking Judge Perry </h3><p>It's interesting that U.S. District Judge April Perry is presiding over the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/11/05/broadview-six-prosecutor-asks-judge-to-delay-high-stakes-hearing-where-feds-could-take-the-stand" >“Broadview Six” case</a> that's tied to the future of Andrew Boutros as U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Illinois — an appointment Perry originally received from former President Joe Biden but then was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/04/24/j-d-vance-block-april-perry-nomination-u-s-attorney-federal-bench-maga-trump-editorial" >blocked</a> by then-Ohio Sen. JD Vance as political retribution for criminal prosecutions against Donald Trump</p><p>In the end Perry, who is qualified to be a U.S. attorney, became a district judge, Boutros became a controversial U.S attorney, and Vance earned one of the strikes against him as Trump's vice president and now as a probable candidate for president.</p><p><i>Ed Stone, Northbrook</i></p><h3>Keep big money out of Chicago elections </h3><p>In the weeks preceding the midterms, well before results came in for Chicago’s first-ever fully elected school board race, one thing was clear: Our democracy had been sold to the highest bidder.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/16/michael-sacks-profile-chicago-billionaire-mayoral-race-brandon-johnson-alexi-giannoulias-rahm-emanuel" >Michael Sacks</a>, chairman and CEO of GCM Grosvenor who is worth an estimated $2 billion, <a class="Link" href="https://www.publicgoodpolicy.org/who-funded-chicago-school-board-2026" target="_blank" ><u>spent nearly $6.5 million </u></a>to influence the school board race through the Common Ground Collective super PAC. In the final stretch, Sacks <a class="Link" href="https://illinoissunshine.org/search/?term=Michael%20Sacks&table_name=candidates&table_name=committees&table_name=officers&table_name=receipts&table_name=expenditures" target="_blank" ><u>gave $700,000</u></a> to<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/chicago-school-board-president-results" > Jessica Biggs</a>’ in her bid to become Chicago Public Schools Board president. The next largest spender in the election was retired executive Jim Frank, with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/16/cash-floods-cps-school-board-races-with-big-money-groups-outraising-the-chicago-teachers-union-5-to-1" >$3.8 million</a>. Together, the two men <a class="Link" href="https://www.publicgoodpolicy.org/who-funded-chicago-school-board-2026" target="_blank" ><u>accounted for 46% of total school board spending</u></a>, outspending the Service Employees International Union and Chicago Teachers Union combined by more than 4 to 1.</p><p>Small-dollar donors accounted for less than 1%.</p><p>Regardless of partisan affiliation, most Americans agree that allowing individuals to sway elections through unlimited spending is a sign of a broken system. And this moment is about more than Sacks. It's about who gets to shape our democracy, whose voices matter and whether ordinary Chicagoans have a meaningful say in decisions affecting their communities.</p><p>For everyday Chicagoans like us who aren't billionaires or corporate executives, contributing $20 or $50 to a candidate we believe in often requires real sacrifice. We give because we believe that candidate represents us. We vote because we believe every voice should carry equal weight, regardless of income or background.</p><p>But that's not how the system works now. Sacks and Frank along with financier Paul Finnegan and the Walton family (yes, Walmart largest shareholders) have leveraged their personal wealth to exert influence over Chicago elections far beyond the power of their individual votes.</p><p>Chicago needs a fair election system —one that could level the playing field for candidates and voters, give candidates with fewer resources a fair chance to compete and rein in the influence of outside moneyed interests.</p><p>The question facing Chicagoans is whether we will accept the appearance of democracy or finally confront the concentrated wealth working to diminish our voices. Because a democracy in which wealth determines who gets heard is a democracy in name only.</p><p><i>Anabel Mendoza,</i> <i>founder, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.democracyunbought.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Democracy Unbought</i></a></p><p><i>Ishan Daya, co-founder and co-executive director, </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.publicgoodpolicy.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Institute for the Public Good </i></a></p><h3>Increasing e-bike, scooter safety</h3><p>As we build bike lanes — and expand shared electric bicycle and scooter use — we face the same challenges other cities have with rider behavior: tourists riding on the sidewalk, teens tripling up on scooters and newbies with noise-canceling headphones blowing through stop signs. As much as we might sometimes want evolution to run its course, we shouldn’t have to wait that long, as there is a better way to improve atrocious Lime and Divvy rider behavior: require the operators to build a secure, community reporting feature into their apps as a condition of their upcoming contract renewal.</p><p>This is technically very doable: Allow someone witnessing unsafe riding to submit a photo or short video directly through the Lime or Divvy app. With the recording’s time and location data, Divvy and Lime could cross-reference that information with its own vehicle location and trip records to assess the complaint, and where the evidence supports it, identify the associated rider account.</p><p>That review would happen privately within the company. The person reporting would never receive the rider’s identity or trip information, and the rider would not receive the reporter’s identity. Just like with parking tickets, these reports could be contested (and reviewed by humans where appropriate), and there would be ample warnings and mandatory safety rules refreshers before a violator could use e-bikes or scooters again. But continued violations could lead to temporary suspension, and ultimately, loss of riding privileges, with responses proportionate to severity and repetition.</p><p>We need shared bikes and scooters. They contribute directly to a reduction in traffic and the cancer-causing emissions cars produce. They aren’t going anywhere. They're only increasing in popularity, so we need to get serious about how we expect people to use them. Sidewalk riding and dangerous behavior undermine public confidence and make walking more stressful, especially for older adults, people with disabilities and families with young children. We can and should require that the giant companies that provide and profit from this equipment include the mechanisms for making their widespread use safer for everyone.</p><p><i>Cyrus Dowlatshahi, Humboldt Park</i></p><h3>No to Peoples Gas </h3><p>With the cost of living continuing to rise, many Chicago residents are already struggling to keep up with their monthly expenses. Peoples Gas is asking for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/business/2026/10/08/peoples-gas-rate-hike-icc-regulatory-judges-recommendation" >$144 million dollar rate increase</a>, which could make monthly bills increase $6 to $8 more. While this may not seem like a lot, it could add unnecessary stress on families and individuals who are already struggling financially. As winter approaches, this means some Chicagoans will have to decide between buying groceries or heating their homes, a choice nobody should have to make.</p><p>As a society shifting to sustainable energy, should we really be investing in infrastructure that will prolong our use of fossil fuels for another century? People’s Gas wants us to remain dependent on their product and by replacing these pipes now, it will make the transition to clean energy more costly and difficult. I believe that this gives us an opportunity to explore other options to fuel our city instead of continuing to rely on fossil fuels. We need to make the right decisions today to provide a future for generations to come. The effects of climate change have become apparent. But it's not too late. Chicago can set an example for communities around the world to take this crisis seriously and invest in energy sources that don't destroy our planet.</p><p>I believe the Illinois Commerce Commission should reject this rate increase. Chicago residents should not carry the cost burden for a company’s expensive projects, especially when those investments will make it harder to move toward more sustainable energy. Enough is enough!</p><p><i>Meredith Holland, Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Prison reform needed, but prisoners should do time </h3><p>Nobody should be incarcerated in a living hell hole. Yes we have a necessity to lock criminals up, but prisons must be humane. Psychiatric services, medical care, education and safety must all be provided. In-prison gangs must be dismantled and separated in order to destroy them. Nonviolent and low-level offenders must never have to face prison gangs for protection or worse.</p><p>At the same time, inmates should serve their full sentence . I favor strong prison reforms, not dismantling them, as we have folks that are just noncompliant to the laws of our society and dangerous to society .</p><p><i>Mike F. Zaczek, Orland Park</i><br></p>

entries.title: What should be done to address traffic on the Kennedy Expressway? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>We asked reader what should be done to address <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/10/23/kennedy-expressway-construction-commuters-illinois-department-transportation-pritzker" >traffic on the Kennedy Expressway</a>? Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>"Stack another deck of lanes on top."<br><i>— Robert Ibarra</i></p><p>"More frequent trains, both Metra and CTA, bus-only lanes for express service on major streets, more protected bike lanes."<br><i>— Thomas Russell</i></p><p>"Charge a toll to subsidize mass transit."<br><i>— Roger Alan Pick</i></p><p>"Incentives from business for more work from home and different hours. Incentives for drivers to not drive during certain times. More park-and-ride areas. Easier connections with the northern L lines."<br><i>— Terri Lynn Visovatti</i></p><p>"Teach people what the left lane is for."<br><i>— David Hernandez</i></p><p>"A second loop to tie our L arteries together at a much larger radius."<br><i>— Eric Q Rosentreter</i></p><p>"Run the express lanes inbound in the evening. That’s when inbound travel times are the highest."<br><i>— Brian Bell</i></p><p>"More and better train and bus service and bike infrastructure. Tolls. ... More accessible train stations. ... You just can't keep pushing more cars on the expressways because no matter how many cars the expressway can move, there are still bottlenecks for cars at the ramps, on the surface grid and in terms of parking. entries.title: It's true: Black Friday deals are starting even earlier than previous years
entries.summary: <p>Retailers are preparing for Thanksgiving weekend — when consumers get to experience the biggest shopping days of the year, spanning from Black Friday to Cyber Monday. But some gave shoppers an early start by offering holiday deals before Halloween decor had a chance to hit the clearance aisle. </p><p>This year in particular, retailers have been starting their Black Friday sales even earlier to entice consumers who are feeling weathered by rising inflation and higher costs for essentials like food and gas.</p><p>On Friday afternoon, a steady stream of shoppers walked inside an Old Navy in Lincoln Park. The store at 1730 W. Fullerton Ave. advertised early Black Friday deals of up to 50%, but most shoppers were unaware of the holiday deals.</p><p>Kayla Burron, 29, and her friend, Taylor Wilkerson, were rifling through racks of sweaters on their day off.</p><p>“I don’t feel like the sales are any different right now,” Wilkerson said.</p><p>Burron snagged a set of holiday pajamas, but not as a gift.</p><p>“I don’t plan to even do any specific Black Friday shopping, just my regular shopping right now,” she said.</p><p>Morgan Majopian was at the store to make a return and ended up with a cart full of winter children’s clothes, including a shiny pink kids puffer vest and a tiny brown sweater dress for her daughter.</p><p>“I used to go Downtown a lot for Black Friday, to Nordstrom, with my mom and sister,” she said. “But most of the time I just shop online now.”</p><p>The mom of two was unaware of the advertised early holiday sale.</p><p>“But I’m going to take advantage of these sales,” she said. “Because I don’t want to be around all those people for Black Friday.”</p><p>This holiday season is marred by economic uncertainty. In Chicago, the average price for a gallon of regular gas soared to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/04/30/chicago-gas-prices-up-iran-war-5-gallon" >more than $5 in May</a>. Prices dropped this week to around $4.70, but it's still elevated compared to a year ago when gas cost $3.60, according to AAA. </p><p>As the Iran war continues to upend the oil industry, diesel prices have also spiked, recently hitting an all-time high in Chicago on Oct. 25 at $7.03 per gallon. Experts have said higher diesel prices are often <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/05/23/diesel-fuel-prices-truckers-farmers-companies-shoppers-gas-price" >passed on to consumers</a> that show up as pricier services and goods like food and shipping fees.</p><p>And the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers reported consumer sentiment was at 48 in October — slightly higher than the all-time low of 44.8<b> </b>in May. The survey dates back to 1952 and is closely watched by economists.</p><p>"We just came off an election where affordability is an issue. So I think there's also a sensitivity to trying to position deals earlier, knowing that consumers are going to potentially have more limited budgets for the holidays," Illinois Retail Merchants Association CEO Rob Karr said. "I think there's also concern [among retailers] about what Washington will or will not do as it relates to tariffs and supply chains."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" name="image-720000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5b5dda5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2Fb2%2Feb57bfa1452c91e765133f6b0d60%2Fblackfriday-261115-011.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6f1aa08/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2Fb2%2Feb57bfa1452c91e765133f6b0d60%2Fblackfriday-261115-011.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/26fda46/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6624x3718+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2Fb2%2Feb57bfa1452c91e765133f6b0d60%2Fblackfriday-261115-011.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Shoppers leave a Target in the Loop, 1101 W. Since 2022, retail spending in October has been higher than September, with a projected a 16.4% gap this year, likely due to Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days last month, according to Adobe Digital Insight’s holiday forecast.</p><p>Activewear brand Alo started touting a 30% sale on Oct. 26. Bolingbrook-based beauty retailer Ulta rolled out weekly deals on Oct. 25, advertising "early Black Friday" discounts of up to 50% off premium brands, a holiday promotion it has done for several years.</p><p>“Retailers are very conscientious about price and value,” Matt Adams, Chicago-based principal at accounting firm Deloitte, said. “Value is not only about price, but other experiences and convenience and things like that. And they're recognizing that consumers are just wanting to make sure that their dollar is going as far as possible, and so they're very conscientious about the prices that they're offering.”</p><p>Target advertised a three-day early Black Friday sale last week, and other major retailers, from Gap and Old Navy to Walmart, have started peddling its early Black Friday sales.</p><p>“While the consumer is willing to spend now, at some point they may not be,” Karr said. “In the competitive nature of the retail sector, it's making those deals affordable, while the consumer is in a spending mood, because no one knows when that will end or what will end it.”</p><p>The National Retail Federation projects retail spending will reach $1 trillion in November and December, a 4.2% year-over-year increase. entries.title: Illinois Republicans crash and burn in the burbs
entries.summary: <p>You may recall that after the March primary I took a look at the results and made the obvious conclusion that the Chicago suburbs were trending ever harder toward the Democrats.</p><p>“Legislative Republicans are right to be afraid of another suburban wipeout,” I concluded at the time.</p><p>Turns out, I underestimated the breadth of the wipeout.</p><p>I didn’t bother to look at McHenry County’s primary results back then. That was a mistake. JB Pritzker became the first Democratic gubernatorial candidate to win McHenry County since 1852. Yes, 174 years ago.</p><p>Indeed, the entire statewide Democratic ticket carried McHenry this month. Pritzker and U.S. Senate candidate Juliana Stratton won by 11 points, and the rest of the ticket won by anywhere from 9 to 18 points (Alexi Giannoulias, who lost the county four years ago, won by 3 points).xf</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-990000" name="module-990000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>Two years ago, Rep. Marty McLaughlin, R-Lake Barrington, defeated Maria Peterson by 4 points in McHenry, and then lost to Peterson this month in the county by more than 10 points. Four years ago, Democrat Allena Barbato lost the 32nd Senate District McHenry precincts to Sen. Craig Wilcox, R-McHenry<b>,</b> by 12 points. This year, she defeated the Republican incumbent in the same precincts by 6 points. Both Democrats went on to win their races.</p><p>This was all pretty predictable had I looked at the primary totals. Democratic primary votes for governor were up by about 60% this year in McHenry County compared to four years ago, while Republican gubernatorial primary totals dropped by 48% or so.</p><p>And unless you’ve been hiding under a rock, you know that formula roughly predicted the rest of the suburban vote this month.</p><p>In DuPage County, the number of Republicans casting primary ballots for governor fell about 33% compared to four years ago. Pritzker is winning that former Republican bastion by almost two-to-one (63-33). He won DuPage four years ago by 15 points (56-41).</p><p>As recently as 2018, DuPage was still a swing county. No more.</p><p>In Lake County this November, not a single statewide Democrat took fewer than 66% of the vote. Earlier this year, Republican primary gubernatorial turnout collapsed by more than 48% compared to four years ago, while Democratic turnout rose by more than 27%. Back in 2014, the county voted for as many statewide Republicans as Democrats.</p><p>Throughout the suburbs, Democratic primary election gubernatorial votes rose by whopping amounts, and that predicted a corresponding but smaller increase in the Democratic general election vote.</p><p>President Donald Trump decided awhile ago to deliberately nationalize the politics of this off-year election and forcefully turn the attention on himself and his proclaimed accomplishments. He even said multiple times that people should vote as if he were on the ballot himself.</p><p>Trump had hoped to do all this to motivate his base and attempt to stir up its turnout to near-presidential election levels and overcome the usual lean toward nonpresidential party candidates in off-years.</p><p>That obviously backfired.</p><p>All Democratic legislative candidates involved in hard-fought campaigns lashed together Trump and their Republican opponents, with an occasional dash of Jeffrey Epstein thrown in for good measure. It didn’t matter if Republicans had no direct ties to Trump or Epstein, they’re Republicans, and that’s more than enough for their purposes. And it worked. Both chambers have picked up several seats.</p><p>Off-year elections have regularly been nationalized over the years. I covered my first such election in 1994, when Republicans won races in downstate and Southern Illinois that nobody thought they’d ever win.</p><p>The truth is there’s very little that the party under fire can do in elections like that. So, all the hindsight now of raising more money, and changing some Republican rhetoric here and there, and recruiting better candidates and strengthening the state party really wouldn’t have worked. Several strong Republican incumbents lost this year and raised enough money to compete. It was the voters what done it.</p><p>It may sting to hear this for some, but what hurts the Republican Party the most is Republicans themselves. They nominated Darren Bailey, who was wiped out by 22 points, and they supported Trump (or refused to criticize him), who dragged everyone else down with his historically awful approval ratings.</p><p>I do not see how the Republicans stand a snowball’s chance in Hades of winning consistently in this state until Republicans themselves decide to move on from this era. Illinois Democrats could get away with losing the South as long as they firmed up the suburbs. Republicans are stuck now as mainly a regional party.</p><p><i>Rich Miller also publishes Capitol Fax, a daily political newsletter, and CapitolFax.com.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c50000" name="module-c50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Insurance money brings with it greed and discord
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My sister-in-law "Leah" has been a poor money manager all her life. She is in significant credit card debt and had to borrow money to help pay for her wedding, despite the fact that she has been a teacher for decades. She has never been a saver — always a spender.</p><p>When my husband passed away recently, he left me with $1 million in life insurance proceeds. When Leah found out about it (I'm not sure how), she asked me to lend her some money to get back on her feet. When I refused, my other sister-in-law chastised me, saying that my husband would have lent her the money. Leah has been bailed out a few times by her sister but never by my husband. Am I wrong to stand my ground? — <i>NOT AN ENABLER</i></p><p><b>DEAR NOT AN ENABLER:</b> My heart goes out to you for the loss of your husband. Leah may be using the word "lend," but believe me when I say you would never see that money again. If she wants to get out of debt, she needs to speak to a credit counselor, not her brother's grieving widow. If she brings it up again, tell her to visit the National Foundation for Credit Counseling at nfcc.org.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 70-year-old divorced man. For the past 10 years, my ex-wife has been living with me. Due to her medical condition and lack of family support, she has no one else to assist her. My own health is declining, so caring for her is a physical strain and emotionally stressful. She refuses any suggestion of a senior living facility because her only income is a small Social Security benefit.</p><p>How do I move on without fighting and accusations? I know I facilitated this by allowing her into my home in the first place. Any ideas where to begin? — <i>FRUSTRATED IN TEXAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRUSTRATED:</b> You were kind to take in and care for your ex a decade ago, but this arrangement is now affecting your health. To protect your own well-being, you must put your foot down. Help your ex-wife one last time by finding her a facility she can afford. Do not expect the transition to be pleasant, but the result will be an improvement for both of you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a happily married woman who went through a midlife crisis more than 20 years ago. At the time, I left my husband for another man, who gave me an expensive cocktail ring. When my relationship with the new man started to suffer for various reasons, I returned to my husband. Our marriage has remained strong ever since.</p><p>I have never worn the ring and have always felt guilty for having it. Should I contact my former lover and return it? Should I pawn it and send him the proceeds? Or maybe you have another suggestion? — <i>RINGS HOLLOW IN ARIZONA</i></p><p><b>DEAR RINGS HOLLOW:</b> Sell the ring and donate the proceeds to a worthy charitable cause. Do not open the door to further contact with your former lover.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: El-Sayed breaks barrier for Muslims who've been in U.S. for half a millennium
entries.summary: <p>Muslims have never been strangers to this country, contrary to the skewed perception of many Americans.</p><p>In 1528 — nearly a century before English colonists <a class="Link" href="https://www.jyfmuseums.org/visit/jamestown-settlement" target="_blank" >arrived</a> in Jamestown and the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/race-and-ethnicity-virus-outbreak-england-wrestling-racial-injustice-956aeb8a01b9a2453d079c681caa9192" target="_blank" >Mayflower</a> dropped anchor in Cape Cod — Mustafa Zemmouri, a <a class="Link" href=" https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20260527-estevanico-the-african-explorer-who-crossed-north-america" target="_blank" >Muslim Moroccan</a>, also known as <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/4c15ba978fcc411dbbdc01f7493f895f" target="_blank" >Estebanico or Estevanico</a>, set foot on what is now the United States.</p><p>The enslaved, Arabic-speaking explorer, whose last name is also written <a class="Link" href="https://muslimamericanheritage.org/recovered-roots/" target="_blank" >Azemmouri</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/muslims-were-part-of-americas-story-long-before-the-republic-began-285895" target="_blank" >walked</a> across the American South, Southwest and into Mexico, serving as a translator and cultural mediator between the Indigenous communities and the Spaniards he traveled with.</p><p>Zemmouri, who may have been killed by the Zuni tribe <a class="Link" href="https://toronto.citynews.ca/2018/02/26/mystery-confines-estebanico-black-explorer-of-us-southwest/" target="_blank" >or</a> faked his death to escape bondage, wasn't an <a class="Link" href="https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/stories/african-muslims-early-america" target="_blank" >anomaly</a>. </p><p>Scholars estimate that as many as <a class="Link" href="https://www.historynewsnetwork.org/article/muslims-arrived-in-america-400-years-ago-as-part-o" target="_blank" >30%</a> of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/wnet/african-americans-many-rivers-to-cross/history/how-many-slaves-landed-in-the-us/" target="_blank" >thousands</a> of other Africans brought to our shores against their will<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://religionnews.com/2026/06/23/how-enslaved-african-muslims-resisted-bondage-through-their-faith-and-writing/" target="_blank" >shared Zemmouri’s Islamic faith</a>, which they were forced to practice in secret or abandon.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-1a0000" name="module-1a0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>I feel compelled to give this history lesson as I watch many fellow Americans <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/15/muslim-politics-democrat-trump-el-sayed-mamdani-piker-rummana-hussain" >freak out </a>over the political rise of Muslims, including Abdul El-Sayed's milestone Senate win in Michigan less than two weeks ago.</p><p>The centuries-old context is particularly significant to El-Sayed's victory, which would have been impossible without the <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/black-michiganders-helped-push-abdul-el-sayed-to-victory-but-the-numbers-show-he-was-less-popular-with-this-key-voting-bloc-than-some-other-democratic-candidates-289777" target="_blank" >votes of Black Michiganders</a>, many of whom are also <a class="Link" href="https://azcir.org/news/2025/05/09/does-phoenix-have-three-times-as-many-mosques-as-detroit-no/" target="_blank" >Muslim</a>.</p><p>There was skepticism before the midterm elections about whether the former public health official of Egyptian descent could garner enough support in Detroit, where the tension between Black and Middle Eastern populations is well-documented. </p><p>The progressive El-Sayed didn't shy away from broaching the subject. He called out anti-Black racism in many Arab and Muslim spaces<b> </b>and credited the Civil Rights Movement for helping bring his family to the U.S. from North Africa — a region where Zemmouri was born 500 years ago. </p><p>"In the Arab and Muslim community, too often people don't really quite appreciate the history on which they walk," El-Sayed <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr1c445TsQo" target="_blank" >told</a> Chicago-born rapper <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/10/29/review-vic-mensa-innanetape-tour-chicago-show" >Vic Mensa</a> in a video podcast interview in late October.</p> <p>"It was organizing in pews in Black churches that addressed the bounds of immigration that allowed my dad to come here. I owe that debt of gratitude (to the Black community)."</p><p>Days later, Haley Stevens, who lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary, walked into the type of house of worship El-Sayed referenced and <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrat-haley-stevens-endorses-gops-mike-rogers-in-michigan-senate-race-2-days-before-election" target="_blank" >sidled up</a> next to Senate Republican nominee Mike Rogers.</p><p>Exploiting a Black sanctum to set the stage for a betrayal is pretty offensive. But for a white woman to use such a site to debut her newfound enthusiasm for a candidate whose party peddles white supremacy is next-level wack.</p><p>I know many Americans were traumatized by the congresswoman's endorsement of the MAGA-aligned Rogers, who used racialized and anti-Muslim rhetoric against El-Sayed.</p><p>For most Muslims, the stunt was an extra punch in the gut and additional proof that some Americans, including those who claim to have our best interests at heart, don't want us in key positions of power. </p><p>After all, it was only a year ago that the Democratic establishment played a starring role in trying to derail Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign in New York City.</p><h3>Hope coupled with despair </h3><p>That Mamdani and El-Sayed prevailed in spite of the vitriol and desperate efforts to block their ascent made their victories even sweeter. Their triumphs symbolize the beauty of a diverse America and its potential to fulfill the promise of equality. But the men's visibility also lays bare the ugliness of bigotry and double standards brandished to render Muslims a threat. </p><p>I'm sure someone started a drinking game somewhere tied to the number of times <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_KE73oJF0us&t=30s" target="_blank" >Mamdani</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/abdul-el-sayed-jewish-palestinian-children-vrtc" target="_blank" >El-Sayed</a> are pressed about their commitment to Jewish safety due to their Palestinian rights advocacy.</p><p>Maybe they're the wrong people to ask. </p><p>Two days after the midterms, a <a class="Link" href="https://jstreet.org/press/j-street-2026-midterm-poll-finds-strong-enduring-jewish-support-democratic-party-0" target="_blank" >national poll</a> commissioned by J Street, a pro-Israel nonprofit, revealed that the majority of Jewish voters said Israel's actions in Gaza and the West Bank, along with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee’s campaign spending against Israel's critics, increase antisemitism.</p><p>No one should feel unwelcome or at risk.</p><p>I just don't hear journalists repeatedly asking politicians what plans they put in place to make Muslims feel safer when they green light bombing Muslim countries and implement policies like the USA Patriot Act that harm our communities at home.</p><p>The first Muslims, who<a class="Link" href="https://www.voanews.com/a/america-s-first-muslims-were-slaves/4763323.html" target="_blank" > helped build the </a>nation with their non-Muslim brothers and sisters, used their voice and written word to resist oppression and document their own and their shackled peers' humanity and intellect.</p><p>Many of us have adopted such traditions to keep persevering. We refuse to be silenced and take solace in knowing that many of our fellow Americans are finally willing to listen and trust us enough to govern in a land where we've existed all along.</p><p><i>Rummana Hussain is a columnist and leads the opinion coverage at the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d40000" name="module-d40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Cancellations, delays at O'Hare, Midway continue Saturday in fallout from yesterday's ground stop
entries.summary: <p>Cancellations and delays continued to affect passengers flying in and out of Chicago's two airports Saturday morning, fallout from Friday's nationwide ground stop.</p><p>As of about 9:30 a.m., 153 flights scheduled to leave O'Hare International Airport on Saturday had been canceled and another 114 had been delayed. The cancellations represented about 11% of scheduled flights, the delays about 8%.</p><p>At Midway International Airport, 25 flights scheduled to depart had been canceled with another 13 flight delayed.</p><h3>Shipping delays may affect package deliveries</h3><h3></h3><p>The ground stop, which started about 2:30 p.m. and lasted more than four hours Friday, may affect timing of package deliveries.</p><p>The U.S. Postal Service and UPS posted notices on their websites Saturday that customers may experience delays.</p><h3>Airlines slowly recovering</h3><p>Across the U.S., airlines worked to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years that canceled more than 2,500 flights Saturday, spread ripple effects around the world, stranded passengers and forced pro and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.</p><p>New technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours, Trump administration officials said.</p><p>Airports were slowly returning to normal, Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said, with planes taking flight and landing. But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system would likely return to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.</p><p>The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key Federal Aviation Administration computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.</p><p>Andrew Charlton, an aviation consultant, said the stoppage on Friday had affected about a quarter of the 45,000 flights in the U.S. each day.</p><p>“The knock-on effect of that is incredible,” said Charlton, managing director of Aviation Advocacy. “The aircraft doesn’t just fly from A to B and back to B and then stop. It then moves onto C and then over to E and around and around and around. It is, of course, exacerbated if you’re talking about long-haul flights, international flights over the Atlantic or over the Pacific.”</p><p>Airlines are obligated to offer free rebooking on another flight for travelers who want to continue their journey, or a refund if their flight was canceled and they decide not to take the trip.</p><p><i>Associated Press contributed to this story.</i></p>

entries.title: Bomb found near ethanol plant in Peoria forces evacuations as authorities investigate
entries.summary: <p>A bomb was found near an ethanol plant in Peoria, sparking evacuations of those who live near the industrial site as law enforcement officials investigate, authorities said Saturday.</p><p>The bomb was found Friday afternoon at the BioUrja Renewables facility in Peoria. While officials say the device has since been “rendered safe,” as of Saturday morning, all residents within a 1-mile radius remained under an evacuation notice as officials continued to scour the facility for any other bombs and evidence.</p><p>Meanwhile, shelters have been set up for those displaced by the threat, authorities said.</p><p>“This is a credible threat,” Peoria Police Chief Brad Dixon told reporters just after midnight Saturday. “We need to take the blast radius seriously.”</p><p>FBI Special Agent Ryan Pressley said his agency was investigating, but declined to provide further details.</p><p>“We will work tirelessly to identify the individual responsible and bring them to justice,” he said.</p><p>No arrests have been made at this time and no injuries have been reported.</p><p>Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8iaipdfQ1OE" target="_blank" >WMBD-TV</a> on Friday that BioUrja is “a plant that has ethanol and highly combustible types of chemicals, and so that’s what alarms us.”</p><p>It's not unusual for law enforcement to receive bomb threats and suspicious package calls, but they often don't result in a credible threat even though such calls are taken seriously by officials who must assess and investigate the claims.</p><p>Just earlier this week, hundreds of airline passengers in Europe had their flights diverted or given military escorts after <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/flight-diverted-france-bomb-threat-dublin-rome-6585ff565ee1ccb9f19b73074aa2fec4" target="_blank" >a series of bomb threats</a> that officials have since declared were malicious hoaxes.</p><p>“We understand that this is a disruptive process for our residents and guests,” said Dixon. “We’re asking for the public’s patience while we work to make this area safe.”</p><p>Peoria has a population of around 110,000.</p><p>The BioUrja plant is located along the Illinois River. The company acquired the ethanol plant in 2021.</p>
